title: Valid Number
statement:
Return `true` if the whole string `s` spells a number in the format below, and `false` otherwise. The format has two parts, in this order:

- **Mantissa** (required): an optional `+` or `-`, then either one or more digits optionally followed by a `.` and zero or more further digits, or a `.` followed by one or more digits. So `7`, `7.`, `7.5` and `.5` are fine, but a lone `.` is not.
- **Exponent** (optional): the letter `e` or `E`, then an optional `+` or `-`, then one or more digits. The exponent has no `.`.

No other character may appear anywhere: no spaces, no other letters, and no extra signs or dots.
constraints: s contains only English letters (upper or lower case), digits 0-9, '+', '-' and '.'
notes:
## Intuition

A regular expression for the grammar would work, but the rules are simple enough to check in one left-to-right scan. Each character is legal or not depending on only three facts about what came before it: whether a digit has appeared (in the current part), whether a dot has appeared, and whether the exponent letter has appeared.

## Approach

1. Start `seenDigit`, `seenDot` and `seenExp` as `false`.
2. A digit sets `seenDigit`.
3. A sign is allowed only at the very start or right after `e`/`E`.
4. An `e`/`E` is allowed only once and only after a digit. It sets `seenExp` and resets `seenDigit`, because the exponent needs digits of its own.
5. A dot is allowed only once and never after the exponent letter.
6. Any other character makes the string invalid.
7. At the end the string is valid exactly when the last part has a digit, so return `seenDigit`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "0"`. The single character `'0'` is a digit, so `seenDigit` becomes `true`. The loop ends and the function returns `seenDigit`, which is `true`. For `s = "."` the dot is accepted, but no digit ever appears, so the answer is `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each character is looked at once.
- Space: O(1): only three flags.

## Pitfalls

- Resetting `seenDigit` after `e` is essential, otherwise `"1e"` would be accepted.
- A dot after the exponent (`"99e2.5"`) is invalid, and so is a dot with no digit on either side (`"."`, `"+.e1"`).
- A sign in the middle (`"6+1"`) or two signs (`"--6"`) are invalid; only position 0 or the spot after `e` may hold one.
- Do not lean on `Number()` or `parseFloat`: they accept `"Infinity"`, spaces and hex, which this grammar rejects.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seenDigit` | a digit appeared in the current part (mantissa, or exponent after `e`) |
| `seenDot` | a dot has already been used |
| `seenExp` | the exponent letter has already been used |
| `i`, `ch` | the current position and its character |

narration.2: Track whether the current part (mantissa, later the exponent) has at least one digit.
narration.3: Track whether a dot has been used; only one is allowed.
narration.4: Track whether the exponent letter has been used; only one is allowed.
narration.6: Scan the string once from left to right.
narration.9: Digits are always welcome; note that the current part now has one.
narration.10: A sign is the next possibility.
narration.11: A sign must sit at the very start or right after e/E; anywhere else is an error.
narration.14: An exponent letter is the next possibility.
narration.15: It may appear only once, and only after the mantissa has a digit.
narration.18: Remember that the exponent has started.
narration.19: The exponent needs digits of its own, so start counting again.
narration.21: A second dot, or a dot inside the exponent, breaks the format.
narration.24: Remember that the one allowed dot is used.
narration.26: Any other character (a letter other than e/E) can never be part of a number.
narration.29: Valid exactly when the last part, mantissa or exponent, ended with digits in it.
